title: History of Ayurveda: Vedas, Charaka & Sushruta Samhitas
metaDescription: Ayurveda's history, from its Vedic roots to the classical Sanskrit samhitas — Charaka, Sushruta and Ashtanga Hridaya — and its revival in modern India.
h1: The History of Ayurveda: From the Vedas to the Classical Samhitas
answerCapsule: Ayurveda is one of the world's oldest documented systems of medicine, with roots in the Vedic period of ancient India (roughly 1500–1000 BCE) and a formal literature codified in the classical Sanskrit texts known as the samhitas. Its three foundational works are the Charaka, Sushruta, and Ashtanga Hridaya samhitas.

sections.capsule: Ayurveda grew out of the healing knowledge of ancient India, with its earliest references appearing in the Vedas, especially the Atharvaveda, around 1500–1000 BCE. For centuries this knowledge passed orally through teacher-student lineages before being gathered into written Sanskrit treatises, the samhitas, that still anchor the tradition today.
sections.body:
The word *Ayurveda* comes from two Sanskrit words: *ayus* (life) and *veda* (knowledge) — the "knowledge of life". It is one of the oldest continuously practised systems of medicine in the world [1][2].

Its earliest traces are woven into the **Vedas**, the ancient sacred texts of India. The **Atharvaveda**, usually dated to around 1500–1000 BCE, contains references to ailments, healing plants, and charms that scholars read as an early layer of Indian medical thought. At this stage, though, medicine was not yet a separate, systematised discipline.

For a long period this knowledge lived as an **oral tradition**, carried from teacher (*guru*) to student (*shishya*) and refined through practice. Only later was it collected, organised, and written down in the Sanskrit textbooks we call the *samhitas*. Those texts are where the history of Ayurveda as a documented medical system really begins.

A note on dates: the chronology below reflects the broad ranges scholars work with. Ancient Indian texts were edited and re-copied over centuries, so precise dating is genuinely uncertain, and honest sources give ranges rather than single years [2]. For an overview of the living system these texts describe, see [what is Ayurveda](/what-is-ayurveda).

sections.h2: What are the classical samhitas of Ayurveda?
sections.capsule: The samhitas are the classical Sanskrit textbooks of Ayurveda. The three most authoritative — the Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, and Ashtanga Hridaya — are together called the Brihat-Trayi, the 'Great Triad'. They cover diagnosis, internal medicine, surgery, pharmacology, and daily regimen, and remain the reference works Ayurvedic physicians study today.
sections.body:
A *samhita* is a compilation — a structured collection of teachings. In Ayurveda, three samhitas stand above the rest and are studied together as the **Brihat-Trayi**, the "Great Triad":

| Text | Traditional author | Scholarly dating | Focus |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Charaka Samhita** | Agnivesha, redacted by Charaka | c. 2nd century BCE – 2nd century CE | Internal medicine (*kayachikitsa*), diagnosis, doshas |
| **Sushruta Samhita** | Sushruta | core c. 6th century BCE, later editing | Surgery (*shalya tantra*), anatomy, instruments |
| **Ashtanga Hridaya** | Vagbhata | c. 6th–7th century CE | Concise synthesis of the above; teaching text |

Alongside these, a later group of three works — the **Laghu-Trayi** or "Lesser Triad" (the Madhava Nidana, Sharngadhara Samhita, and Bhavaprakasha) — became important in the medieval period for diagnosis and pharmacy. Together the Brihat-Trayi and Laghu-Trayi form the classical curriculum an Ayurvedic student still meets today. The theory of the three doshas that runs through these texts is explained in our guide to [the three doshas](/doshas).

sections.capsule: The Charaka Samhita is the foundational text of Ayurvedic internal medicine (kayachikitsa). Scholars date its present form to roughly the 2nd century BCE–2nd century CE, built on an older tradition attributed to Agnivesha. It sets out physiology, diagnosis, medical ethics, and the theory of the three doshas that still organises the tradition.
sections.body:
The **Charaka Samhita** is the cornerstone of Ayurvedic internal medicine. Tradition holds that it began as the *Agnivesha Samhita*, the teaching of the sage Agnivesha, and was later redacted by the physician **Charaka** into the form that survives [2].

It is remarkable for how much of it is about *how to think and practise*, not only what to prescribe. Among its themes:

- A detailed account of **physiology and pathology** organised around the three doshas — *vata*, *pitta*, and *kapha*.
- A structured method of **diagnosis** and clinical reasoning.
- A famous section on the **ethics and conduct of the physician** — humility, consent, and care for the patient — that reads strikingly modern.
- Extensive **materia medica**: descriptions of plants, diets, and preparations, and their traditional uses.

The Charaka Samhita is why Ayurveda is often described as a system built on constitution and balance rather than on isolated symptoms.

sections.capsule: The Sushruta Samhita is the classical text of Ayurvedic surgery (shalya tantra). Often dated to a core of around the 6th century BCE with later editing, it describes surgical instruments, techniques, and training methods, and is why Sushruta is frequently called a founding figure of surgery and reconstructive technique in the ancient world.
sections.body:
Where the Charaka Samhita is the great text of internal medicine, the **Sushruta Samhita** is the great text of **surgery** (*shalya tantra*). It is attributed to **Sushruta**, and its surgical core is often traced to around the 6th century BCE, with later editing over subsequent centuries [3].

It is unusually practical for so ancient a text, describing:

- More than a hundred **surgical instruments**, and how to use them.
- Techniques for procedures including the setting of fractures and early **reconstructive methods**, including a technique for repairing the nose that historians of medicine still cite.
- A structured approach to **surgical training**, including practice on models before operating.
- Detailed study of **anatomy** by dissection.

For these reasons Sushruta is frequently described as one of the founding figures of surgery in the ancient world [3]. The text is a reminder that classical Ayurveda was a broad medical system, not only a herbal one.

sections.capsule: The Ashtanga Hridaya, attributed to Vagbhata around the 6th–7th century CE, distils the earlier works of Charaka and Sushruta into a single, well-organised summary. Compact and memorable, it became the most widely studied Ayurvedic text across India and beyond, and remains a core teaching text in Ayurvedic education today.
sections.body:
The **Ashtanga Hridaya** ("the heart of the eight branches") is attributed to **Vagbhata**, usually placed in the 6th–7th century CE. Rather than adding a mass of new material, Vagbhata did something enduringly useful: he **synthesised** the earlier teachings of Charaka and Sushruta into one clear, well-ordered, and memorable text.

That clarity is why it travelled. The Ashtanga Hridaya became one of the most widely copied and studied Ayurvedic works, influential well beyond India, and it remains a **core teaching text** in modern BAMS education. Its companion volume, the more detailed *Ashtanga Sangraha*, is also attributed to Vagbhata.

If you want to see how the therapies these texts describe are structured today, our guide to [panchakarma](/panchakarma) walks through the classical purification procedures still in use.

sections.h2: How was classical Ayurveda organised — the eight branches?
sections.capsule: Classical Ayurveda organises medicine into eight branches, together called Ashtanga Ayurveda: internal medicine, surgery, treatment of the head and neck, paediatrics, toxicology, psychiatry, rejuvenation (rasayana), and reproductive health. This eightfold structure, set out in the samhitas, shows how comprehensive the classical system aimed to be.
sections.body:
The word *ashtanga* means "eight limbs". Classical Ayurveda divided medicine into **eight branches** — the reason Vagbhata's summary is called the Ashtanga Hridaya:

| Branch (Sanskrit) | Field |
|---|---|
| Kayachikitsa | Internal medicine |
| Shalya tantra | Surgery |
| Shalakya tantra | Diseases of the head and neck (eye, ear, nose, throat) |
| Kaumarabhritya | Paediatrics and care in childbirth |
| Agada tantra | Toxicology |
| Bhuta vidya | Psychological and psychiatric conditions |
| Rasayana | Rejuvenation and healthy ageing |
| Vajikarana | Reproductive and sexual health |

Seen together, the eight branches show that classical Ayurveda set out to be a **complete system of medicine**, from surgery to paediatrics to mental health, and not merely a collection of herbal remedies. Whether every branch is supported by modern evidence is a separate question, which we address honestly on [is Ayurveda scientific?](/is-ayurveda-scientific).

sections.h2: How did Ayurveda develop after the classical period?
sections.capsule: After the classical age, Ayurveda continued through medieval compendia such as the Madhava Nidana and Bhavaprakasha, was disrupted during the colonial period, and revived in modern India. Today it is regulated under the Ministry of AYUSH, taught in BAMS degree colleges, and practised alongside conventional medicine as a complement, not a replacement.
sections.body:
The story did not end with the samhitas.

- **Medieval period.** New compendia refined diagnosis and pharmacy. The *Madhava Nidana* became a standard reference on the classification of disease, and the *Bhavaprakasha* an important text on medicinal substances. This is the era of the Laghu-Trayi.
- **Colonial disruption.** Under British rule, state support shifted to Western medicine, and formal Ayurvedic education and institutions were marginalised for a long stretch. The tradition survived largely through family lineages and regional practice — including in **Kerala**, which preserved a distinctive and continuous Ayurvedic culture.
- **Modern revival.** From the twentieth century onwards, Ayurveda was reorganised as a formal discipline: degree colleges awarding the **BAMS** qualification, pharmacopoeial standards, and eventually a dedicated government ministry.
- **Today.** In India, Ayurveda is regulated under the **Ministry of AYUSH** [4] and practised by qualified physicians, increasingly positioned as a **complement to conventional medicine rather than a replacement** [1]. Manufacturing has moved towards audited Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) quality standards, which is directly relevant to modern safety concerns about some Ayurvedic products [1].

sections.h2: How does Kairali read these texts first-hand?
sections.capsule: Because Kairali's physicians train in and practise from these classical texts, this site can explain them from inside the living tradition rather than at second hand. The same panchakarma stages and formulations described in the samhitas are still practised under physician supervision at Kairali's NABH-accredited hospital.
sections.body:
History books describe the samhitas. A practising Ayurvedic organisation reads them as working manuals.

At the **Kairali Ayurvedic Group**, physicians qualify in and practise from these classical texts. The purification procedures set out in the Charaka Samhita, the physician's discipline it insists on, and the formulations catalogued across the tradition are not museum pieces here — they are part of daily clinical work. That is what lets this site explain them from inside the living tradition rather than only from the outside.

Where the samhitas describe therapies, those therapies are practised today under physician supervision at Kairali's NABH-accredited Ayurvedic hospital in Kerala, and the classical formulations are made at the group's GMP-certified pharmacy. We note this as a matter of record, not as a recommendation.

To continue, read the main guide, [what is Ayurveda](/what-is-ayurveda), explore [the three doshas](/doshas) the classical texts describe, or learn [more about who publishes this site](/about).

faqs.a: Ayurveda's roots reach back to the Vedic period of ancient India, roughly 1500–1000 BCE, making it one of the world's oldest documented systems of medicine. Its formal literature, the Sanskrit samhitas, was compiled over the following centuries and is still studied today.

faqs.q: What are the three main classical texts of Ayurveda?
faqs.a: The three foundational texts, known together as the Brihat-Trayi or 'Great Triad', are the Charaka Samhita (internal medicine), the Sushruta Samhita (surgery), and the Ashtanga Hridaya (a concise synthesis by Vagbhata). They remain core references in Ayurvedic education.

Sushruta is the figure to whom the Sushruta Samhita, the classical Ayurvedic text on surgery, is attributed. Its surgical core is often dated to around the 6th century BCE. Because it describes instruments, techniques and reconstructive methods, Sushruta is frequently called a founding figure of surgery.
